questions.prompt: What is the key idea in the aggregate expenditure macroeconomic model?

options.text: In the short run, with the price level fixed, the level of total (planned) spending determines the level of real GDP
In the short run, changes in the price level adjust to make planned spending equal to potential GDP
Real GDP is determined only by the supply of labour, capital and technology
Real GDP always equals potential GDP because prices adjust immediately

questions.explanation: The AE model is a **short-run model that holds the price level constant**: total planned spending (C + I<sub>p</sub> + G + NX) determines real GDP. When spending differs from output, firms see unplanned inventory changes and adjust production, not prices.

questions.prompt: What are inventories, and what usually happens to them at the beginning of a recession and at the beginning of an expansion?

options.text: Goods produced but not yet sold; they fall unexpectedly at the start of a recession and build up at the start of an expansion
Goods produced but not yet sold; they build up unexpectedly at the start of a recession (sales fall short of expectations) and fall unexpectedly at the start of an expansion
Raw materials bought by firms; they are unchanged over the business cycle
Goods already sold but not yet delivered; they rise in both a recession and an expansion

questions.explanation: **Inventories are goods that have been produced but not yet sold.** When a recession starts, sales drop below what firms expected, so unsold goods pile up (unplanned inventory increase). At the start of an expansion sales exceed expectations and firms' inventories are run down unexpectedly.

source.note: The textbook answer is 'the business cycle'; cyclical unemployment is a by-product of the same fluctuations.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does the aggregate expenditure model seek to explain?

options.text: Long-run economic growth
Inflation (the price level is assumed fixed in this model)
The business cycle (short-run fluctuations in real GDP, and the cyclical unemployment that goes with them)
The natural rate of unemployment

questions.explanation: With the price level held constant, the AE model explains **short-run fluctuations in real GDP, i.e. the business cycle**, and so cyclical unemployment. Long-run growth depends on supply-side factors, and inflation requires letting the price level move (AD–AS, later).

questions.prompt: a. The Jones family buys a new car.

options.text: Planned investment (I<sub>p</sub>)
Government purchases (G)
Net exports (NX)
Consumption (C)

questions.explanation: Household purchases of newly produced goods (even big ones like cars) are **consumption**. Only new houses count as household 'investment'.

questions.prompt: b. The Toronto District School Board buys 12 new school buses.

options.text: Government purchases (G)
Consumption (C)
Planned investment (I<sub>p</sub>)
Net exports (NX)

questions.explanation: School boards are part of government; their purchases of goods and services are **government purchases**.

questions.prompt: c. The Jones family buys a newly constructed house from the Garcia Construction Co.

options.text: Consumption (C)
Planned investment (I<sub>p</sub>)
Government purchases (G)
Net exports (NX)

questions.explanation: Newly constructed housing is counted as **investment** (spending on new capital), not consumption.

questions.prompt: Between October and December 2021, inventories increased by roughly $2.5 billion. Can we tell from this whether aggregate expenditure was higher or lower than GDP in those three months?

options.text: Yes. Inventories rose, so AE was lower than GDP
Yes. Inventories rose, so AE was higher than GDP
No. We would also need to know how much of the increase was planned versus unplanned; only an unplanned increase means AE < GDP
No. Inventory changes tell us nothing about the relationship between AE and GDP under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Actual investment = planned investment + **unplanned** change in inventories. Firms may deliberately build inventories (planned investment, already in AE). Only the **unplanned** part signals AE < GDP, so we need the planned versus unplanned breakdown.

questions.prompt: In late 2014 Japanese firms' inventories rose because the drop in demand was 'bigger than expected'. Does it matter that firms didn't expect the drop? Won't a decline in demand always raise inventories?

options.text: It doesn't matter: any fall in demand automatically raises inventories by the same amount
It matters only for exports, not for domestic sales
It doesn't matter: firms never adjust production in the short run
It matters: only an unexpected shortfall in sales raises inventories involuntarily; if firms foresee lower demand they cut production and inventories need not rise

questions.explanation: Unplanned inventory investment is the signal that production must fall. If firms **anticipate** weaker demand they cut output ahead of time, so inventories needn't build up. Hence a decline in demand does not always produce an inventory increase; the **unexpected** part does.

questions.prompt: In the AE model, why is it important to know the factors that determine consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports?

options.text: Changes in these factors change aggregate expenditure and therefore equilibrium real GDP, so they let us predict (and respond to) fluctuations in GDP
They are needed only to measure last year's GDP, not to explain changes in it
Because they determine the price level, which is the key variable in the model
Because they fix potential GDP in the short run

questions.explanation: Real GDP is determined by AE = C + I<sub>p</sub> + G + NX, so understanding **what shifts each component** lets us forecast how a shock changes equilibrium GDP.

questions.prompt: Which list gives one example of each of the four categories of aggregate expenditure (C, I<sub>p</sub>, G, NX)?

options.text: A household buys a new house; a firm buys shares of stock; a city pays pensions to retirees; a Canadian buys a US car
A household buys a TV; a firm buys a new machine; a city buys snow ploughs; Canadian lumber is sold to the US (an export)
A household buys a used car; a firm hires workers; the federal government pays EI benefits; a Canadian sells shares abroad
A household buys a TV; a firm buys corporate bonds; the government pays student grants; Canada imports oil

questions.explanation: C = household purchases of goods/services; I<sub>p</sub> = firm purchases of capital goods (and new housing); G = government purchases of goods and services (**not transfers**); NX = exports − imports. Stocks, bonds, used goods and transfer payments are not any of these.

questions.prompt: What are the main determinants of planned investment, and how does a change in interest rates affect it?

options.text: Current disposable income, wealth, the price level and the exchange rate; a higher interest rate raises investment
The exchange rate, foreign GDP and relative prices; interest rates have no effect
Expectations of future profitability, the real interest rate, taxes and cash flow; a higher real interest rate reduces investment, a lower one increases it
Expectations, taxes, cash flow and the MPC; a higher interest rate raises investment because it raises returns on savings

questions.explanation: Planned investment depends on **expected profitability, the real interest rate, taxes and cash flow**. Higher real interest rates raise the cost of borrowing, so fewer projects are profitable and investment falls.

questions.prompt: What are the three main determinants of net exports? How would an increase in the growth rate of GDP in developing countries affect Canadian net exports?

options.text: Relative price levels, relative GDP growth rates and the exchange rate; faster growth abroad raises Canadian imports, so net exports fall
Canadian disposable income, wealth and interest rates; faster growth abroad has no effect
Relative price levels, taxes and cash flow; faster growth abroad lowers Canadian exports
Relative price levels, relative GDP growth rates and the exchange rate; faster growth abroad raises foreign demand for Canadian goods, so Canadian net exports rise

questions.explanation: NX depends on **Canadian vs foreign price levels, Canadian vs foreign GDP growth, and the exchange rate**. Faster growth abroad raises foreign incomes, increasing demand for Canadian exports (and not Canadian imports), so NX rises.

questions.prompt: a. A survey shows a sharp rise in consumer confidence that income growth will be increasing.

options.text: The forecast of demand will be revised upward
The forecast of demand will be revised downward
The forecast is unaffected
Cannot be determined without knowing the MPC

questions.explanation: Higher expected future income raises consumption now, so demand for Tim Hortons' products is forecast to **rise**.

questions.prompt: b. Real interest rates are expected to increase.

options.text: The forecast of demand will be revised upward
The forecast of demand will be revised downward
The forecast is unaffected
Cannot be determined without knowing the MPC

questions.explanation: Higher real interest rates reduce consumption of durables and discourage investment, lowering spending: forecast **down**.

source.note: Textbook reasoning runs through net exports; for a domestic coffee chain the effect is indirect.

questions.prompt: c. The exchange rate value of the Canadian dollar is expected to increase.

options.text: The forecast of demand will be revised upward
The forecast is unaffected
The forecast of demand will be revised downward
Cannot be determined without knowing the MPC

questions.explanation: A higher Canadian dollar makes Canadian goods more expensive abroad and imports cheaper, so NX falls and aggregate spending on Canadian-produced goods falls: forecast **down**.

questions.prompt: d. Planned investment spending in the economy is expected to decrease.

options.text: The forecast of demand will be revised upward
The forecast is unaffected
Cannot be determined without knowing the MPC
The forecast of demand will be revised downward

questions.explanation: Lower I<sub>p</sub> reduces AE and (through the multiplier) income, so spending on Tim Hortons' products is forecast to fall.

questions.prompt: a. An increase in current income causes…

options.text: A movement along the consumption function (to a higher point on the same line)
An upward shift of the consumption function
A downward shift of the consumption function
A change in the slope (the MPC)

questions.explanation: Income is the variable on the horizontal axis, so a change in it moves us **along** the consumption function. The slope is the MPC.

questions.prompt: b. An increase in expected future income or in household wealth causes…

options.text: A movement up along the same consumption function
An upward shift of the consumption function (more consumption at every level of current income)
A downward shift of the consumption function
No change, because only current income affects consumption

questions.explanation: Expected future income and wealth are determinants of consumption **other than current income**, so changing them **shifts** the whole function up.

questions.prompt: Does the existence of employment insurance make it likely that consumption will fluctuate more or less over the business cycle than without it?

options.text: More: EI encourages workers to quit, so consumption is more volatile
More: EI payments are counted as government purchases
Less: EI payments support the disposable income of unemployed workers, so their consumption falls by less in a recession
No difference: consumption depends only on the interest rate

questions.explanation: EI is a transfer that props up disposable income when output and jobs fall, so **consumption fluctuates less** (an automatic stabilizer).

questions.prompt: Why might a small business owner pay for detailed consumer confidence data (such as the Consumer Confidence Index)?

options.text: Confidence data directly measure the firm's profit
Confidence affects only government purchases
Because consumer confidence always predicts GDP perfectly
Confidence affects expected future income and hence consumption, so the data help the owner forecast demand for the firm's products

questions.explanation: Expectations of future income are a **determinant of consumption**; the index helps the owner forecast spending (and plan inventory, hiring, etc.).

questions.prompt: a. Saving when Y = 900 (billions).
questions.explanation: With taxes zero, S = Y − C = 900 − 800 = **100**.

questions.prompt: b. Saving when Y = 1100 (billions).
c. Saving when Y = 1300 (billions).
d. What is the MPC (same in every row)?
e. What is the MPS?
Should a local home building company pay attention to reports of Canadian GDP? Why or why not?

options.text: Yes: housing demand depends on the state of the economy (income, confidence) and interest rates, so GDP reports signal changes in demand for new homes
No: housing construction is independent of the business cycle
No: GDP reports only measure government purchases
Yes, but only because GDP directly sets the price of lumber

questions.explanation: New housing is part of investment and is **cyclical**: it falls in recessions (weak incomes, pessimism) and rises in expansions. GDP reports therefore help the builder forecast demand.

questions.prompt: A student objects: 'The chapter said a higher interest rate lowers investment, but if I can get a higher rate I'll invest more in my savings account.' Do you agree?

options.text: Yes: a higher interest rate raises both saving and firms' investment
No: 'investment' in the AE model means firms' spending on capital goods and new housing, which is discouraged by higher borrowing costs; putting money in a savings account is saving, not investment
Yes: investment in the model means buying financial assets
No: interest rates have no effect on any kind of spending

questions.explanation: In macroeconomics **investment = purchases of new physical capital (and new housing)**, not financial assets. A higher interest rate raises the cost of financing those projects, so planned investment falls.

questions.prompt: a. What does Gurría mean by 'conventional trade statistics'?

options.text: Statistics on the value added by each country in a product
Statistics on only domestic sales
Statistics that record the gross value of exports and imports each time goods cross a border
Statistics on exchange rates

questions.explanation: Conventional statistics count the **full (gross) value** of goods each time they cross a border.

questions.prompt: b. Why might they be less reliable than they once were?

options.text: Because countries no longer trade with each other
Because exchange rates are fixed
Because imports are now always zero
Global value chains: parts cross borders several times, so the same value is counted repeatedly and the value added by each country is obscured

questions.explanation: With production split across countries, intermediate goods are counted at **every crossing** (double counting), overstating how much any country actually adds.

questions.prompt: c. What problems could this cause for policymakers?

options.text: They may misjudge trade balances and who gains from trade, leading to misguided trade policy
Policymakers would be unable to collect any taxes
Policymakers would think exchange rates are too stable
There would be no problems; gross figures are always accurate

questions.explanation: Misleading numbers about bilateral deficits and dependence can lead to **poorly targeted tariffs or trade agreements**.

questions.prompt: What is the meaning of the 45° line in the 45°-line diagram?

options.text: It shows all points where consumption equals saving
It shows all points where aggregate expenditure equals real GDP, i.e. every possible macroeconomic equilibrium
It is the aggregate expenditure function
It shows potential GDP

questions.explanation: Both axes have the same units, so the 45° line is the set of points where **AE = GDP**. The actual equilibrium is where the AE line crosses it.

questions.prompt: In a 45°-line diagram (AE on the vertical axis, real GDP on the horizontal), where is macroeconomic equilibrium?

options.text: Where the AE line crosses the vertical axis
At the highest point on the AE line
Where the upward-sloping AE line crosses the 45° line; equilibrium real GDP is read from the horizontal axis at that point
Where the 45° line crosses the horizontal axis

questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires AE = GDP, so it lies on the 45° line **and** on the AE line: their intersection. Label the horizontal coordinate Y*.

questions.prompt: What does the slope of the AE line equal, and how is it related to the slope of the consumption function?

options.text: 1 − MPC; it is steeper than the consumption function
The multiplier; it is flatter than the consumption function
Zero; I<sub>p</sub>, G and NX are constant
The MPC; it is the same as the slope of the consumption function (the AE line is the consumption function shifted up by I<sub>p</sub> + G + NX)

questions.explanation: Only C depends on GDP; I<sub>p</sub>, G and NX are constants. Each extra $1 of GDP raises AE by the **MPC**, so the AE line is **parallel** to the consumption function.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between aggregate expenditure and consumption spending?

options.text: Aggregate expenditure = C + I<sub>p</sub> + G + NX; consumption is just one component
They are the same thing in a closed economy
Aggregate expenditure excludes consumption
Consumption includes investment and government purchases

questions.explanation: AE is **total planned spending**; consumption is its largest part (about 55% of GDP in 2024) but not all of it.

questions.prompt: What is likely to happen if firms have large unplanned inventory investments?

options.text: Firms raise production and hire more workers
Firms cut production (and employment), so GDP falls until AE and GDP are equal
Prices fall immediately and restore equilibrium
Nothing; unplanned inventories do not affect production

questions.explanation: Unplanned inventory build-up means AE < GDP. With prices fixed, firms respond by **reducing output and employment**.

source.note: The figure is not reproduced; the point labels given in the textbook are used.

questions.prompt: a. At point A, planned aggregate expenditure is…

options.text: Less than GDP (an unintended increase in inventories)
Equal to GDP
Greater than GDP (an unintended decrease in inventories)
Impossible to determine

questions.explanation: At A firms have **unintended inventory decreases**: sales exceed production, so AE > GDP. The vertical distance between AE and the 45° line measures the unintended inventory change.

questions.prompt: b. At point B (on the 45° line), planned aggregate expenditure is…

options.text: Greater than GDP
Less than GDP
Equal to potential GDP by definition
Equal to GDP (macroeconomic equilibrium, no unintended inventory change)

questions.explanation: On the 45° line AE = GDP: firms sell exactly what they expected to, so there is **no unplanned inventory change**.

questions.prompt: c. At point C, planned aggregate expenditure is…

options.text: Less than GDP (an unintended increase in inventories)
Greater than GDP (an unintended decrease)
Equal to GDP
Equal to zero

questions.explanation: At C production exceeds planned spending, so AE < GDP and unplanned inventories **rise**. Firms then cut output.

questions.prompt: If net exports depend on real GDP, does the line relating NX to real GDP have a positive or negative slope?

options.text: Positive: higher GDP raises income and therefore exports
Negative: higher GDP raises income and therefore imports, which lowers net exports
Positive: higher GDP raises the exchange rate
Zero: net exports never depend on GDP

questions.explanation: Higher Canadian GDP raises spending on imports (while foreign demand for exports depends on foreign GDP), so NX = X − M **falls as Y rises**.

source.note: The 2009 Q4 value is shown as printed in the source table (same as Q3).

questions.prompt: Which explanation best fits the pattern of inventory investment?

options.text: Inventories fall at the start of a recession and rise throughout it, because firms stockpile goods
Inventory investment is unrelated to the business cycle

As the recession began, sales fell short of expectations and inventories built up unintentionally; firms then cut production and ran inventories down (negative values in 2009); inventory investment rebounded as the expansion resumed
Inventories were negative in 2009 because GDP was above potential

questions.explanation: The pattern is **cyclical**: unplanned build-ups when sales unexpectedly slump (2008), liquidation of stocks during the recession (2009–early 2010), and rebuilding during recovery (2011–12).

questions.prompt: a. What is the value of the MPC?
Fill in the table. What is planned aggregate expenditure when Y = 1100?
What is the unplanned change in inventories when Y = 1000? (Negative = decrease.)
questions.explanation: At Y = 1000: AE = 840 + 200 = 1,040. Unplanned inventory change = Y − AE = 1000 − 1040 = **−40**.

questions.prompt: b. What is the value of equilibrium real GDP?
questions.explanation: AE = C + 200 and C rises 0.8 per $1 of Y. At Y = 1200, C = 1000 and AE = 1,200 = Y. Unplanned inventory change is zero, so Y* = **1,200**.

questions.prompt: Do you agree: 'The equilibrium level of GDP is determined by AE. Therefore, GDP will decline only if households decide to spend less on goods and services.'?

options.text: Agree: only consumption matters because it is the largest component
Agree: investment, G and NX are fixed by definition
Disagree: GDP is determined by the price level, not by spending
Disagree: a decline in any component of AE (investment, government purchases or net exports), not just consumption, can lower equilibrium GDP

questions.explanation: AE = C + I<sub>p</sub> + G + NX. A fall in **any** autonomous component (and the multiplier) lowers equilibrium GDP.

questions.prompt: What is the multiplier effect? What does it imply for a $100 million decrease in government purchases?

options.text: An autonomous change in spending leads to a larger change in equilibrium GDP; the decrease shifts the AE line down and lowers GDP by more than $100 million
An autonomous change in spending changes GDP by exactly the same amount; GDP falls by $100 million
A change in GDP changes the price level; GDP falls by less than $100 million
It applies only to increases in spending, so GDP is unchanged

questions.explanation: A fall in G lowers income, which **induces** a further fall in consumption, and so on; the total fall in GDP = multiplier × ΔG, which is larger than |ΔG| (when MPC > 0). On the 45° diagram the AE line shifts down and the intersection moves left.

questions.prompt: What is the multiplier formula, and why is it considered too simple?

options.text: 1/MPC; it ignores the role of saving
1/(1 − MPC); it ignores that imports, income taxes, interest rates and the price level also respond to income changes, which reduce the real-world multiplier
MPC/(1 − MPC); it ignores consumption
1/(1 + MPC); it ignores government purchases

questions.explanation: Multiplier = **1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS**. In reality part of extra income is lost to imports and taxes, and higher output raises interest rates and prices, so the actual multiplier is smaller.

questions.prompt: a. The movement from A to B (along AE₁) represents…

options.text: A change in autonomous expenditure
No change in aggregate expenditure
A change in induced expenditure (spending changes because GDP changes)
A change in the MPC

questions.explanation: A movement **along** one AE line is caused by a change in GDP, so it is an **induced** change.

questions.prompt: b. The movement from B to C (to the higher line AE₂) represents…

options.text: A change in induced expenditure
A movement along the AE line
A change in the slope of the AE line
A change in autonomous expenditure (a shift of the AE line, not caused by GDP)

questions.explanation: A shift of the AE line is an **autonomous** change: spending changes at every level of GDP (e.g. due to I<sub>p</sub>, G or NX).

questions.prompt: a. If real GDP increases to $3,250 billion, is the economy in equilibrium?

options.text: No: at Y = 3,250 consumption rises, so AE exceeds 3,250 and inventories fall unexpectedly
Yes: AE = 3,250 so AE = GDP
No: AE falls below GDP and inventories build up
Yes: the multiplier is zero in the short run

questions.explanation: The extra $250 of income induces more consumption, so AE rises further and **AE > GDP**; production keeps rising.

source.note: MPC = 0.5 is implied by Figure 8.12 itself: a $250 billion rise in investment raises equilibrium GDP from 3,000 to 3,500 (multiplier 2).

questions.prompt: b. With MPC = 0.5, what is aggregate expenditure (billions) when real GDP is 3,250?
questions.explanation: GDP rises 250 from 3,000, so C rises 0.5 × 250 = 125. AE = 3,250 + 125 = **3,375**, still above GDP. Process continues to Y* = 3,500.

questions.prompt: a. What is the equilibrium level of real GDP?
b. What is the MPC?
c. Net exports increase by $40 billion. What is the new equilibrium level of real GDP?
a. By how much (billions) does the AE line shift up?
questions.explanation: A change in planned investment is a change in autonomous expenditure: the AE line shifts up by exactly **$40 billion**.

questions.prompt: b. By how much (billions) does equilibrium real GDP increase?
a. An increase in real GDP increases imports. True or false: this makes the multiplier smaller.
questions.explanation: Higher imports are a leakage: less of each extra dollar of income is spent on domestic goods, so the effective MPC is lower and the multiplier **smaller**.

questions.prompt: b. An increase in real GDP increases interest rates. True or false: this makes the multiplier smaller.
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates reduce investment and durable consumption, offsetting part of the initial increase: the multiplier is **smaller**.

questions.prompt: c. An increase in real GDP increases the MPC. True or false: this makes the multiplier larger.
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC); a larger MPC means a **larger** multiplier.

questions.prompt: d. An increase in real GDP causes the average tax rate paid by households to decrease. True or false: this makes the multiplier larger.
questions.explanation: Lower taxes leave households more disposable income per dollar of GDP, so more is spent; the multiplier is **larger**.

questions.prompt: e. An increase in real GDP increases the price level. True or false: this makes the multiplier larger.
questions.explanation: A rising price level reduces wealth, exports and so on, damping the rise in real GDP: the multiplier is **smaller**, not larger.

questions.prompt: Booming economies in developing countries cause Canadian net exports to rise by $75 billion. If the MPC is 0.8, what is the change in equilibrium GDP (billions)?
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5; ΔY = 5 × 75 = **$375 billion**.

questions.prompt: Would a larger multiplier lead to longer and more severe recessions, or shorter and less severe ones?

options.text: Less severe recessions: a larger multiplier cushions falls in spending
More severe (deeper) recessions: a given fall in autonomous spending causes a larger fall in GDP
No effect: the multiplier works only for increases in spending
Shorter recessions, because GDP falls faster and then recovers at once

questions.explanation: The multiplier works **in both directions**. A larger multiplier magnifies any negative shock to autonomous spending, so recessions tend to be **deeper**.

questions.prompt: Why might the multiplier for non-residential construction be 1.52 in Quebec but only 1.07 in Nunavut?

options.text: Nunavut households have a higher MPC
Nunavut has more domestic suppliers than Quebec
Quebec's larger, more diversified economy produces more of its inputs and consumer goods locally, so less of each extra dollar leaks into imports than in Nunavut
Quebec has no taxes, so the multiplier is larger

questions.explanation: Multipliers are smaller when more income is spent on **imports from outside the region** (leakage). Remote Nunavut imports most inputs and goods.

questions.prompt: a. What would analysts and politicians mean by 'multiplier'?

options.text: The factory's number of employees
The ratio of Tesla's profits to its investment
The increase in the price level
The total increase in GDP and jobs resulting from the factory spending, as a multiple of the initial investment

questions.explanation: The multiplier is **change in equilibrium GDP ÷ initial change in autonomous spending**.

questions.prompt: b. Why would Tesla's investment significantly boost Ontario's and Canada's economy?

options.text: Construction and equipment spending raise incomes of workers and suppliers, who then spend more, inducing further rounds of consumption
Because investment spending is exempt from the multiplier
Because Tesla spends only outside Canada
Because it lowers the price level

questions.explanation: Investment is **autonomous spending**; the incomes it generates induce consumption, so GDP rises by more than the initial outlay.

questions.prompt: c. Why might analysts and politicians be unsure of the size of the multiplier?

options.text: Because the multiplier formula is exactly 1/(1 − MPC) and nobody knows the MPC
The size depends on the MPC, import content, taxes and other leakages and on how much of the spending is local, all of which are hard to know in advance
Because the multiplier is always exactly 1
Because factories are not part of GDP

questions.explanation: The simple formula overstates real-world multipliers; **import content, taxes, and interest-rate and price responses** are uncertain.

questions.prompt: 'Europe is entering its fifth consecutive year of growth, supported by … robust business and consumer confidence, and improving world trade.' Which components of AE are affected and why does GDP grow?

options.text: Confidence raises government purchases; world trade raises consumption; the AE line shifts down
Only net exports are affected; the AE line is unchanged
Confidence raises consumption and planned investment; improving world trade raises net exports. The AE line shifts up, so equilibrium GDP rises (by a multiple of the autonomous increase)
Confidence lowers investment; world trade lowers net exports

questions.explanation: Optimism raises **C and I<sub>p</sub>**, and stronger foreign demand raises **NX**. All are autonomous increases that shift the AE line up and move the equilibrium to the right on the 45° diagram.

questions.prompt: McKinsey estimated that raising US infrastructure spending by $150 billion to $180 billion per year would raise GDP by $270 billion to $320 billion. What is the implied multiplier (approximately)?
questions.explanation: Multiplier = ΔY/ΔG: 270/150 = 1.8 and 320/180 ≈ 1.78. The implied multiplier is about **1.8**.

questions.prompt: Briefly, what is the difference between aggregate expenditure and aggregate demand?

options.text: AE shows the price level at each real GDP; AD shows spending at a given price level
They are identical
AE includes only consumption; AD includes all four components
AE is total planned spending at a given real GDP (price level fixed); AD shows the quantity of real GDP demanded at each price level

questions.explanation: AE relates **spending to GDP** (price level held constant); the AD curve relates **real GDP demanded to the price level**.

questions.prompt: Which components of aggregate expenditure are affected by a change in the price level?

options.text: Consumption, planned investment and net exports
Only consumption
Consumption and government purchases
Only government purchases and net exports

questions.explanation: A higher price level lowers real wealth (C), raises interest rates (I<sub>p</sub>), and raises Canadian prices relative to foreign ones (NX). Government purchases are set by policy and don't respond.

questions.prompt: Does a change in the price level cause a movement along or a shift of the AE line? Along or a shift of the AD curve?

options.text: It moves along the AE line and shifts the AD curve
It shifts the AE line, and moves us along the AD curve
It shifts both
It moves along both

questions.explanation: A new price level changes C, I<sub>p</sub> and NX **at every GDP**, so the AE line shifts. Each point of AD is the equilibrium for one price level, so a price change is a **movement along AD**.

questions.prompt: Why is the AE line upward sloping while the AD curve is downward sloping?

options.text: AE slopes up because higher prices raise spending; AD slopes down because higher GDP lowers prices
Both slope up
AE slopes up because higher GDP raises income and consumption; AD slopes down because a higher price level lowers C, I<sub>p</sub> and NX, lowering equilibrium GDP
AD slopes down because government purchases fall as prices rise

questions.explanation: Different axes, different mechanisms: **AE vs GDP** (income effect on C) versus **price level vs GDP demanded** (wealth, interest-rate and net-export effects).

questions.prompt: Do you agree: 'The AD curve slopes downward because when the price level is higher, people cannot afford to buy as many goods and services.'?

options.text: Yes: higher prices reduce people's incomes proportionally
Yes: because the AD curve is derived from the budget constraint
No: because the AD curve is actually upward sloping
No: higher prices come with higher incomes, so affordability isn't the reason; the downward slope reflects the wealth, interest-rate and international-trade effects

questions.explanation: In the macro economy one person's price is another's income; the AD slope comes from the **wealth effect, the interest-rate effect and the exchange-rate/net-export effect**.

questions.prompt: Suppose exports become more sensitive to price-level changes in Canada. Will AD become steeper or less steep?

options.text: Less steep (flatter): a given rise in the price level now reduces exports, and so GDP demanded, by more
Steeper
No change
It shifts right without changing slope

questions.explanation: A bigger response of NX to P makes the AE line shift more for a given change in P, so real GDP demanded changes by more: AD is **flatter**.

questions.prompt: Write the AE function in general form. As a line on the 45° diagram, what are its intercept and slope?

options.text: AE = MPC + (C̄ + Ī<sub>p</sub> + Ḡ + NX̄)Y; intercept = MPC, slope = autonomous expenditure
AE = (C̄ + Ī<sub>p</sub> + Ḡ + NX̄) + MPC × Y; intercept = autonomous expenditure, slope = MPC
AE = (C̄ + Ī<sub>p</sub> + Ḡ + NX̄)/(1 − MPC); intercept = 0, slope = 1
AE = Y; intercept 0 and slope 1

questions.explanation: Substituting C = C̄ + MPC·Y gives AE = (C̄ + I + G + NX) + MPC·Y: **intercept = autonomous expenditure, slope = MPC**.
